paragraphs: ## 1. A Voyage Already in Danger

Mary Shelley's Frankenstein follows an ambitious student who brings a living being into existence and then refuses the relationship his achievement creates. This complete summary and reading review follows the novel's 1831 text, while recognising that the work first appeared in 1818. Victor Frankenstein is the creator; the creature receives no personal name. The narrative moves between their competing accounts of suffering and responsibility, beginning far from the laboratory. Before readers learn how the creature was made, they encounter a frozen landscape in which both creation and creator have almost reached the limits of survival.

Robert Walton, an English explorer, describes his northern expedition in letters to his sister, Margaret Saville. He hopes to discover an Arctic passage and contribute to scientific knowledge, but public benefit is entangled with his desire for exceptional achievement. He imagines the unknown region with an enthusiasm that outruns the evidence available to him. His letters also reveal loneliness. Although he commands a crew, he longs for an educated companion who can understand his ambitions and correct his judgement. The expedition therefore begins with two connected needs: to accomplish something extraordinary and to be recognised by someone capable of appreciating it.

While ice surrounds the ship, the sailors notice an unusually large figure driving a sledge across the distant surface. Soon afterwards, they rescue another traveller, exhausted and close to death. This man is Victor Frankenstein. Remarkably, he asks where the ship is going before agreeing to come aboard: even rescue matters to him chiefly as a means of continuing his pursuit. Walton nurses him and quickly develops an intense admiration for his intelligence and sensitivity. The reader, however, has already seen the material result of whatever Victor once hoped to achieve: a damaged man following another being through a landscape almost empty of human life.

When Walton speaks about the knowledge he hopes to gain, Victor recognises an ambition resembling his own. He offers his history as a warning. Yet the circumstances complicate that warning from the beginning. Walton regards Victor as the friend he has been seeking, so he is predisposed to admire the speaker before evaluating the story. Victor is also looking backwards through grief, choosing which incidents explain his ruin. His account may contain sincere regret and attempts to justify himself at the same time. Shelley invites the reader to listen sympathetically without surrendering independent judgement.

The novel's structure matters because information passes through several hands. Walton records Victor's narrative for Margaret; within it, Victor reproduces the creature's account of experiences he did not witness. Letters and other documents offer supporting material, but no detached narrator settles every disagreement. Reading becomes an exercise in weighing testimony. The Arctic frame also establishes a practical question that will return at the end: can a person recognise the cost of ambition early enough to change direction? Walton still has a crew to protect and a sister to return to. Victor's opportunity to choose differently belongs mostly to the past.
## 2. Affection, Education, and the Desire to Discover

Victor recalls a privileged childhood in Geneva. His father, Alphonse, is respected and affectionate; his mother, Caroline, has known poverty and responds generously to vulnerable people. In the 1831 version, Elizabeth Lavenza is the daughter of an Italian nobleman and a German mother. After her mother's death and her father's disappearance, she lives with a poor foster family in Italy until Caroline brings her into the Frankenstein household. Elizabeth is raised alongside Victor, although she is not his biological cousin. The family sometimes uses the language of cousinship, and Victor describes her with a troubling mixture of affection, admiration, and possession.

Another important companion is Henry Clerval, whose imaginative interests include heroic adventures, literature, and languages. Elizabeth is associated with domestic affection and the beauty of the natural world, while Victor increasingly wants to uncover the principles beneath appearances. These differences do not make his early life unhappy. On the contrary, his account emphasises the security he receives from family and friendship. This background makes his later abandonment of the creature especially striking. He understands, through experience, what patient care can provide, yet fails to offer even the beginnings of such care to the being wholly dependent on him.

As a boy, Victor becomes fascinated by older writers on natural philosophy and alchemy. Their promise of hidden powers appeals to his desire for discoveries beyond ordinary human limits. His father's brief dismissal of these books does little to explain their weaknesses, leaving curiosity without adequate guidance. Later encounters with modern explanations of electricity and natural processes redirect his interests. Looking back, Victor repeatedly presents educational accidents and chance meetings as decisive turns towards disaster. That retrospective pattern deserves attention: it can illuminate the circumstances that shaped him, but it can also make deliberate choices appear to have been unavoidable.

Before Victor leaves for university at Ingolstadt, Elizabeth contracts scarlet fever. Caroline nurses her, becomes ill herself, and dies. On her deathbed, she expresses the hope that Victor and Elizabeth will eventually marry. Her death interrupts a household that has seemed protected from severe loss. Victor mourns, postpones his departure, and then resumes his education. It would be too simple to explain his entire scientific ambition as an immediate response to bereavement, since that ambition already exists. Nevertheless, the loss gives particular emotional force to a project concerned with the boundary between living bodies and dead matter.

At university, Professor Krempe dismisses Victor's earlier studies harshly, while Professor Waldman offers a more generous account of scientific progress. Waldman acknowledges the ambitions of earlier thinkers while praising the practical achievements of modern chemistry. His encouragement helps Victor commit himself to intensive study. Victor makes rapid progress, becomes absorbed in the structure of living organisms, and begins investigating decay. He eventually believes he has discovered how to produce life. He does not disclose a reproducible method to Walton. The novel concentrates on the consequences of possessing this knowledge, rather than supplying a technical account of the procedure itself.
## 3. The Achievement Victor Cannot Bear

Victor begins constructing a human figure. Because working with tiny structures would be difficult, he makes the body much larger than an ordinary person's. He gathers materials through disturbing investigations of bodies and biological processes, withdrawing from company as his work advances. The important change is not simply that his experiment is unusual. His sense of proportion deteriorates: ordinary obligations become distractions, affection seems less urgent than completion, and physical exhaustion becomes an acceptable price. He imagines a new kind of being grateful to him for its existence, but gives little sustained thought to what that being might need once alive.

This imagined gratitude reveals a central imbalance. Victor pictures himself receiving recognition as a creator before he considers the experience of the created person. He has plans for an achievement, not for a relationship. Meanwhile, he neglects letters from home and loses the restorative contact with nature that previously gave him pleasure. The project takes over his days and nights until completion seems to promise release from every difficulty it has produced. Shelley makes the process feel less like confident mastery than narrowing attention: the closer Victor comes to his goal, the less of the surrounding world he allows himself to see.

On a November night, the creature begins to breathe and move. Victor immediately recoils from the appearance of the body he has assembled. Features that he selected individually do not create the beauty he expected, and animation intensifies his disgust. He retreats, sleeps briefly, and experiences a nightmare in which Elizabeth becomes associated with his dead mother. Waking, he sees the creature near his bed, attempting contact. Victor interprets its presence through terror and flees. The being's first moments of conscious life are therefore marked by the disappearance of the only person who knows how it came into existence.

Henry Clerval arrives in Ingolstadt soon afterwards, having obtained permission to pursue further study. Victor returns with him to the apartment and finds that the creature has gone. His relief does not lead him to search for it or consider its survival. Instead, the strain of his work and the shock of its result overwhelm him, and he falls seriously ill. Henry nurses him through a prolonged recovery, protecting him from unnecessary disturbance and gradually helping him reconnect with everyday life. The contrast is direct: Victor survives because another person undertakes the patient care that he has refused to provide.

During his recovery, Victor turns away from the scientific subjects that now provoke distress. He shares Henry's interest in languages and literature, receives news from Elizabeth, and begins to enjoy walks again. These quieter passages demonstrate that friendship and attention can restore someone whose identity has narrowed around a single obsession. Yet recovery also permits avoidance. Victor treats the creature's absence as if it had removed the underlying problem, although no arrangement has been made for its welfare or for the safety of others. His private horror remains private, and the consequences of his experiment develop beyond his knowledge.
## 4. William and Justine: Private Knowledge, Public Harm

A letter from Alphonse ends this fragile period of recovery. Victor's youngest brother, William, has been murdered near Geneva. Returning home, Victor reaches the city too late to enter its closed gates and walks near the place where the child died. During a storm, lightning reveals the creature. Victor immediately concludes that it killed William. At this point he has not heard a confession or seen the murder; his certainty comes from recognising the being and connecting its presence with the crime. The distinction between conviction and evidence matters, even though the creature will later confirm his conclusion.

Victor then learns that Justine Moritz, a young woman closely attached to the family, has been accused. A miniature portrait that William carried was discovered in her clothing. Other circumstances, including her movements during the night and her distressed behaviour, are interpreted against her. The reader sees how a plausible account can harden around incomplete evidence. Justine's confusion becomes a sign of guilt rather than a response to exhaustion and grief. Her previous kindness offers little protection once the court and public have organised the available facts into a story of criminal intention.

Elizabeth speaks in Justine's defence, insisting that the accusation contradicts the character she knows. Victor, however, does not reveal the experiment or the creature's existence. He believes his account would be dismissed as madness and would fail to save the accused woman. That concern is understandable within the world of the novel, but it does not remove the moral problem. He possesses information that nobody else can assess because he withholds it. His inward certainty that he is responsible produces intense suffering, yet suffering is not equivalent to taking action on another person's behalf.

Justine is convicted. Under religious pressure and fear of being denied spiritual comfort, she confesses to a crime she has not committed. She subsequently tells Elizabeth and Victor that the confession is false. Her execution completes the second death connected to William's murder. Shelley gives this episode consequences beyond Victor's personal anguish: a child has been killed, an innocent woman has been condemned, and legal and religious authorities have helped transform vulnerability into apparent guilt. Elizabeth's faith in the goodness of people is shaken. The family cannot simply resume its former understanding of the world.

Victor describes himself as the concealed cause of these disasters and struggles with despair. Seeking relief, he travels into the Alps, where immense natural scenes temporarily interrupt his inward torment. The mountains offer perspective without supplying a solution. On a glacier near Mont Blanc, the creature approaches him with extraordinary speed and strength. Victor responds with anger and threats, but the creature insists that its maker must hear its history. It argues that judgement without a hearing repeats the rejection it has already endured. Victor eventually agrees, and the narrative passes to a voice he had previously treated as incapable of deserving attention.
## 5. An Education from Outside the Door

The creature begins with bewildered sensations rather than a fully formed adult understanding. Light, darkness, hunger, cold, and sound arrive before it can organise them. It discovers food and shelter through trial and error, and learns that fire can provide warmth while also causing pain. These early experiences make its impressive body seem especially misleading: physical strength does not supply knowledge, language, or emotional security. When it approaches people, their fear and violence drive it away. Its education in human society therefore starts with a lesson that its own appearance can provoke punishment before it has done anything wrong.

Eventually, the creature finds a small shelter adjoining a cottage in Germany. Through a gap, it observes the De Lacey family: an elderly blind father, his son Felix, and his daughter Agatha. Their poverty initially puzzles it, as does the sadness beneath their affectionate behaviour. It secretly takes some food, then stops when it realises that doing so increases their hardship. Instead, it gathers wood for them at night. This change is ethically significant. Without direct instruction or the prospect of praise, it recognises another person's need and alters its own conduct to reduce harm.

By listening carefully, the creature begins connecting sounds with objects and actions. Language opens a world that physical observation alone could not explain. When Safie arrives at the cottage and receives lessons in French, the hidden listener benefits from the same teaching. Her presence also makes Felix happier, demonstrating the emotional force of companionship. As the creature learns to read and understand more complex speech, it discovers history, social ranks, property, government, and conflict. Knowledge enlarges its imagination, but it also clarifies its exclusion. It possesses neither family connections nor wealth nor a recognised place within any community.

The De Laceys themselves have suffered injustice. Felix helped Safie's father, a Turkish merchant, escape a death sentence in France that the narrative presents as influenced by prejudice and wealth. In consequence, the De Lacey family lost its position and was exiled. Safie's father encouraged Felix's affection for his daughter when it served the escape, then opposed their union. Safie eventually defied him and travelled to join Felix. The episode gives the creature examples of generosity, betrayal, and independent decision. A critical reading should also recognise that its portrayal of religion and women's freedom relies on sweeping cultural assumptions that readers need not accept.

The creature finds books, including Paradise Lost, Plutarch's Lives, and The Sorrows of Werter, which supply different models of human action and suffering. It reads with intense personal involvement, comparing its situation with beings who have origins, histories, or companions. Paradise Lost makes its isolation particularly painful: even a rejected figure seems to belong to a larger moral story. Papers discovered in the clothes it took from Victor reveal the circumstances of its creation and the maker's disgust. Reading therefore gives it both intellectual resources and documentary evidence that the person responsible for its life found that life repellent.
## 6. Rejection, Violence, and a Demand

The creature hopes that eloquence and good intentions can overcome the response to its appearance. It plans to approach the blind De Lacey while the others are absent, allowing the old man to judge its words before his family judges its body. Their conversation begins promisingly. De Lacey listens to an account of loneliness and offers sympathy, unaware that the strangers whose favour his visitor seeks are his own children. The creature becomes increasingly emotional, and the family's return interrupts the encounter before trust can develop. Felix sees an alarming figure beside his father and attacks it; the creature escapes without fighting back.

For a time, it considers trying again. It recognises that its approach may have been too sudden and hopes the old man's kindness could still provide a path towards acceptance. That possibility vanishes when it learns that the frightened family has left the cottage permanently. It burns the abandoned building in anger. The act marks a change from helping people secretly to destroying the place associated with its disappointed hopes. The family is absent when the fire is set. Its violence is already serious, but the distinction prevents this episode from being confused with a murder of the De Laceys.

Using information in Victor's papers, the creature travels towards Geneva to find its creator. During the journey, it rescues a girl who has fallen into a river. A man who sees it with her responds by shooting it, interpreting rescue as danger. The creature experiences this as another demonstration that kindness cannot overcome the judgement imposed on its body. Its wound heals, but resentment deepens. Shelley supplies strong reasons for understanding that resentment while continuing to show the creature making choices. Being treated unjustly explains its growing hatred; it does not establish that every later victim deserves punishment.

Near Geneva, the creature encounters William and imagines that a child might be young enough to accept it. Its attempt to force companionship on him immediately contradicts that hope. William struggles, insults its appearance, and identifies his family. On hearing the name Frankenstein, the creature recognises an opportunity to injure Victor through someone he loves. It strangles the boy and takes the miniature portrait. Later, finding Justine asleep, it places the portrait in her clothing. This is deliberate manipulation of evidence. The creature's account confirms both William's murder and its role in directing suspicion towards an innocent woman.

After completing its narrative, the creature demands that Victor create a female companion of the same kind. It promises that they will leave human society and live remotely in South America, surviving without harming people. The request combines a powerful appeal to loneliness with coercion: refusal will bring further suffering. Victor initially rejects it, then becomes persuaded that he owes some remedy to the being he abandoned. He also hopes that agreement will protect his family. His consent resolves the immediate confrontation without resolving the deeper uncertainties, including whether a second conscious being could reasonably be bound by an agreement made before her existence.
## 7. A Promise Withdrawn

Back in Geneva, Victor struggles to resume ordinary relationships while carrying the obligation he has accepted. Alphonse hopes that marriage to Elizabeth will ease his distress, but Victor feels unable to marry before completing the new creature. He arranges to travel to Britain, where he can consult scientific knowledge useful to the task. Henry accompanies him, delighted by opportunities for learning and acquaintance. Their contrasting responses to travel expose the narrowing of Victor's life. Henry sees people, landscapes, and possibilities; Victor sees delays, threats, and the work he is reluctant to perform.

The journey takes them through parts of continental Europe to England, and later north into Scotland. Victor eventually separates from Henry and chooses a remote island in the Orkneys for his secret work. The setting provides privacy but also intensifies the isolation that characterised the first experiment. This time he proceeds without the earlier confidence. The materials and actions disgust him, and the future he once treated as a space for glorious achievement becomes a field of possible disasters. He cannot know whether the promised withdrawal from humanity will occur or whether creating another being will multiply the danger.

Victor's doubts grow more specific. The female creature might reject the male, refuse the arrangement imposed on her, or develop desires neither existing party can predict. The pair might have children, bringing into existence a population humans could be unable to control. Some fears concern genuine uncertainty; others assume hostility from a being who has not yet lived. The scene therefore creates an ethical conflict rather than an easy answer. Keeping his promise would affect someone unable to consent to its terms, while breaking it would destroy the only hope he has offered to the creature already alive.

Seeing the creature watching through the window, Victor tears apart the unfinished female body. She has never been animated. The creature witnesses the destruction and later confronts him, treating the act as the deliberate cancellation of its future. Victor refuses to reconsider. Their exchange abandons the limited negotiation they previously achieved, and the creature threatens to appear on Victor's wedding night. Victor assumes that the threat concerns his own death. This interpretation fits his tendency to place himself at the centre of every conflict, although the creature has already demonstrated that it can hurt him by attacking others.

Victor takes the remains out to sea in a boat and disposes of them. After falling asleep, he is carried away and eventually lands in Ireland, where local people suspect him of a recent murder. The victim is Henry Clerval, whose body bears signs of strangulation. Confronted with his friend's corpse, Victor collapses and suffers another severe illness. The magistrate, Mr Kirwin, treats him with consideration, and Alphonse comes to support him. Evidence eventually establishes that Victor was elsewhere when Henry died, allowing his release. Legal innocence, however, offers little relief from his sense that the secret struggle has destroyed another person who cared for him.
## 8. The Wedding and the Pursuit

Victor returns towards Geneva with his father, burdened by Henry's death and the creature's threat. Elizabeth writes to ask whether he loves someone else, interpreting his distance through the ordinary possibilities available to her. She offers to release him from their expected marriage if it would make him unhappy. Her question exposes the cost of his secrecy: she tries to make a generous decision without access to the facts shaping her life. Victor assures her of his love and promises an explanation after the wedding. He postpones disclosure beyond the moment when it might help her judge the danger.

They marry and travel across the lake to spend the night at an inn in Evian. Victor carries weapons and expects an attack on himself. Elizabeth senses his fear but does not understand its source. Hoping to spare her the confrontation, he asks her to retire while he searches the building. Then he hears her scream. The creature has strangled her in their room. Victor's attempt at protection has left her alone with the danger he failed to identify. Seeing the creature at a window, he fires unsuccessfully; the murderer escapes, and the future promised throughout his childhood has been destroyed.

The loss overwhelms Alphonse, who dies soon afterwards. Victor undergoes a period of mental collapse and confinement before recovering enough to act. He eventually tells a magistrate about the creature and demands official assistance. The extraordinary story and the practical difficulty of capturing such a being prevent the response he wants. Victor then commits himself to pursuit. The role reversal is striking: the creator who once fled contact now organises his existence around finding the being he abandoned. Yet pursuit is still a form of fixation, and revenge offers him purpose without restoring any of the relationships he has lost.

The chase leads across great distances and into the north. The creature leaves messages and sometimes supplies that allow Victor to continue. These interventions make the pursuit a relationship of mutual dependence as well as hatred. The creature wants Victor to experience prolonged isolation and suffering; Victor needs the prospect of revenge to keep moving. Neither simply escapes the other. As their route enters increasingly hostile conditions, the external landscape comes to resemble the reduction of their emotional world. Food, movement, endurance, and the enemy ahead replace the wider society both have lost.

On the Arctic ice, Victor nearly catches up, but the breaking surface separates him from the creature. Stranded on a drifting piece of ice, he makes his way to Walton's ship, returning the narrative to its opening situation. The entire history has led to the exhausted stranger whom Walton admired before knowing his name. Victor asks Walton to continue the pursuit if he dies. His story thus functions in two directions: it warns against destructive ambition, while also attempting to recruit a new person into an unfinished act of revenge. The reader must assess the conflict between the lesson Victor claims to teach and the obligation he now tries to pass on.
## 9. What Walton Chooses, and What Remains Unknown

Walton's own expedition becomes increasingly dangerous as ice traps the ship and threatens the crew. Representatives of the sailors ask him to promise that, if a passage opens, he will return south instead of pressing forward. Their demand forces the question that Victor repeatedly avoided: how much can a leader ask other people to risk for an ambition they do not fully share? Victor intervenes with an eloquent speech urging perseverance and portraying retreat as shameful. The dying man who has described the cost of obsession can still make the language of heroic achievement sound irresistible.

Walton eventually agrees to return. His decision should not be confused with a complete emotional conversion. He remains disappointed and initially regards the crew's determination as a defeat imposed on him. Nevertheless, his action matters more than perfect acceptance. He recognises that he cannot justly drive unwilling people into further danger. When the ice opens, the ship turns towards home. Unlike Victor, Walton permits a relationship with other people to place an effective limit on his project. He loses the result he wanted, but preserves possibilities that the novel's central adversaries have progressively destroyed.

Victor weakens and dies aboard the ship. Before his death, he reflects on his conduct, acknowledges some duties towards the creature, and continues to defend his refusal to make a companion. His advice remains divided: he recommends a quieter happiness, then admits that another ambitious person might succeed where he failed. Walton mourns him deeply. The narrative does not provide a final speech that resolves every contradiction in Victor's character. His tenderness, intelligence, pride, suffering, and capacity for self-justification remain present together, even as his ability to act comes to an end.

Afterwards, Walton finds the creature beside Victor's body. It expresses grief and remorse, insisting that revenge has brought torment rather than satisfaction. Walton challenges this account, pointing out that remorse did not prevent repeated murder. The creature describes the deterioration of its earlier hopes into hatred, but also recognises the horror of what it has done. Its final appearance asks the reader to hold sympathy and condemnation together. A person may have been profoundly wronged and still be responsible for terrible wrongs. Neither fact has to erase the other.

The creature announces that it intends to travel farther north, build a funeral fire, and burn itself so that no remains will allow another being like it to be made. It then leaves the ship and disappears across the dark water on a piece of ice. Walton does not witness the promised fire or verify the creature's death. The ending therefore contains a declared intention and a final disappearance, rather than a confirmed account of suicide. That limit is consistent with the novel's larger method: the reader receives powerful testimony, but must distinguish what a speaker says from what the narrative actually shows.
## 10. Reading Responsibility beyond the Experiment

The central ethical failure in Frankenstein develops through the separation of technical achievement from continuing care. Victor asks whether he can create life and imagines the status that success will bring. He does not prepare to teach, protect, accompany, or listen to the life he produces. This makes the novel more demanding than a simple warning that knowledge is dangerous. Its scientists are not condemned merely for asking ambitious questions. The catastrophe unfolds when the capacity to act grows faster than the willingness to remain answerable for the consequences, especially once those consequences become frightening or inconvenient.

The creature's education complicates any easy division between a humane society and an inhuman outsider. Before committing murder, it learns sympathy by observing affection, discovers injustice through history, and attempts to help people. Its appearance repeatedly prevents those actions from being recognised. Yet the novel also resists turning exclusion into a complete excuse. William, Justine, Henry, and Elizabeth are individuals, not interchangeable representatives of the society that rejected it. By attacking them to punish Victor, the creature repeats the reduction of persons to instruments that marked its creator's original dream of grateful dependence.

Family relationships reveal another version of this problem. Victor benefits from the labour of people whose ambitions rarely occupy the centre of his account. Caroline nurses, Elizabeth comforts, Justine cares for children, and Henry tends the sick. Their work sustains the conditions in which his intellectual freedom becomes possible. The destruction of the unfinished companion extends the question to a woman denied even the chance to speak. Victor and the creature debate her purpose before she exists. A critical reading can recognise the real danger Victor fears while asking why her imagined independence appears chiefly as a threat to plans made by men.

The competing narratives also make responsibility a matter of language. Victor repeatedly describes himself as driven by fate, while the creature describes its violence as the outcome of rejection. Both explanations contain evidence; both can become ways to reduce personal agency. Walton's admiration supplies another pressure on judgement, encouraging the reader to see Victor through the eyes of a devoted friend. The task is neither to dismiss every narrator nor to accept the most moving speech. It is to notice omissions, compare accounts with actions, and ask whose experience remains outside the speaker's preferred explanation.

Frankenstein leaves its readers with an unresolved but productive tension between understanding and accountability. Its most disturbing figure can speak with intelligence and feel remorse; its gifted, affectionate protagonist can abandon obligations and misunderstand those closest to him. The novel's emotional power depends on preserving that complexity. Walton offers a limited alternative because he changes his conduct while still feeling disappointed. He does not repair Victor's losses or settle the creature's future, but he stops adding unwilling companions to the cost of his ambition. Across the larger tragedy, that imperfect decision gives practical weight to the possibility of learning.

quiz.q: How is Elizabeth connected to Victor's family in the 1831 version followed here?
options: She joins the household after Victor meets her at university.
She is Victor's biological cousin, raised elsewhere until adulthood.
She is brought into the household as a child and raised alongside Victor.
She is Henry Clerval's sister and visits Geneva during his illness.

quiz.q: What does the creature's decision to stop taking food from the De Laceys show?
options: It recognises their hardship and changes its behaviour to reduce harm.
It has already decided that all people deserve to suffer.
It expects the family to reward it publicly for its generosity.
It no longer needs food because it has mastered the use of fire.

quiz.q: Why does Victor destroy the unfinished female creature?
options: Henry discovers the experiment and orders him to abandon it.
He learns that the original creature has already left for South America.
Elizabeth demands that he complete their marriage before continuing.
He fears consequences that neither his promise nor the creature's assurances can control.

quiz.q: What makes Walton's final decision different from Victor's pattern of conduct?
options: He persuades the sailors to accept every danger as the price of discovery.
He allows his responsibility towards unwilling crew members to limit his ambition.
He completes Victor's pursuit before returning to his scientific expedition.
He gives up exploration because he no longer feels any disappointment.

quiz.q: What can readers confidently say about the creature at the end?
options: Walton watches it build a fire and confirms that it dies.
It promises to live peacefully with a new companion in South America.
It announces an intention to burn itself and disappears; its death is not witnessed.
The returning sailors capture it and bring it to trial in England.
